blogs.title: One Definition of “Similarity” to Rule Them All: Federal Circuit Aligns DuPont Factors in Apex Bank v. CC Serve
blogs.description: The court faulted the TTAB for using a narrower notion of “similar” under DuPont factor six than it used under factor two. After finding the parties’ services “highly similar” (indeed, partially legally identical) for the services-overlap inquiry, the Board then limited third‑party-use evidence to credit-card services alone when assessing marketplace crowding. The Federal Circuit held that was legal error, reinforcing Juice Generation and Jack Wolfskin’s teaching that the sixth factor looks to similar—not identical—goods. This post unpacks the doctrinal harmonization across DuPont factors, why internal consistency matters to likelihood-of-confusion analysis, and the practical upshot: applicants can marshal third‑party uses from the full swath of related services once the Board has found those services similar.

blogs.title: Counting “ASPIREs”: How Many Third‑Party Uses Make a Mark Weak?
blogs.description: The TTAB dismissed 42 third‑party “Aspire”-formative uses because they weren’t for credit-card services, leaving only nine uses—too few, it thought, to show weakness. The Federal Circuit vacated that analysis, cautioning against cabin­ing the relevant marketplace and against treating numerical thresholds as talismans. Drawing on Palm Bay, Juice Generation, and Jack Wolfskin, this post explores how tribunals should weigh the number and nature of third‑party uses and registrations, the difference between conceptual and commercial strength, and best practices for building a record (marketplace evidence plus registrations) that can meaningfully narrow a prior registrant’s scope of rights.

blogs.title: Banking on Overlap: Federal Circuit Affirms Broad Similarity Between Credit Cards and “Banking and Financing Services”
blogs.description: On factor two, Apex lost: the court affirmed that credit-card services substantially overlap with “banking and financing services,” relying on dictionary definitions and third‑party registrations, and recognizing industry realities where servicers partner with issuing banks. The post explains why the deletion of the “credit card services” ID Manual entry didn’t save Apex, how outsourcing/partnering models collapse perceived distinctions, and what this means for drafting identifications, prosecuting financial‑services marks, and assessing clearance risk for fintechs and internet‑only banks that don’t yet issue cards but sit close to that lane.

blogs.title: Commercial Impression on a Sliding Scale: Why Factor One Can’t Precede Factor Six
blogs.description: Because the strength or weakness of the shared term shapes commercial impression, the Federal Circuit vacated the TTAB’s factor‑one analysis of ASPIRE vs. ASPIRE BANK pending a proper factor‑six review. This post examines the analytical sequencing: how evidence of a crowded field can shift the first‑factor focus from the shared element to distinguishing matter (e.g., “BANK” and design features), and when it won’t. It offers guidance for brand owners using aspirational terms in finance, and a roadmap for the Board to avoid bootstrapping by reassessing commercial impression only after calibrating marketplace strength.
